title: Words in Freedom: the Ditch outside Milan, the Front Page, and Four Wars
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Alexandria and the French of the Levant

stops.name: Alexandria, birth in the Italian colony
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Filippo Tommaso Emilio Marinetti is born in Alexandria on the twenty-second of December, to Enrico Marinetti, a lawyer out of Voghera in Piedmont, and Amalia Grolli, daughter of a Milanese professor of letters. The Italian record notes that the two never married and lived together more uxorio. The family belongs to the prosperous Italian colony that Egypt's courts and concessions have made rich. French is the language of his schooling, Arabic the language of the street, Italian the language of a country he has not yet seen. No plaque marks the house and the street itself is lost.
suggested_refs: The Italian colony of Alexandria under the Khedivate, whose lawyers and merchants Enrico Marinetti served

stops.name: College Saint-Francois-Xavier, the Jesuits and Papyrus
stops.date_confidence: enters the school 1888 (attested); the Papyrus episode is placed at about age seventeen, month unknown; the campus site is approximate
stops.campa: He enters the Jesuit College Saint-Francois-Xavier as a boarder in 1888 and reads French novels under the desk. At about seventeen he founds a school magazine called Papyrus and fills it with Zola, whom the fathers have not authorized; they threaten him with expulsion. He is not expelled, and some accounts treat the expulsion story as embellished afterwards. He leaves for Paris anyway. The lesson he carries out of the school is that a forbidden page gets read. Behind him the Jesuits go on teaching Latin to the sons of merchants.
suggested_refs: Papyrus, the school magazine, and the Jesuit index of forbidden French novels

stops.name: Paris, the baccalaureate at the Sorbonne
stops.date_confidence: contested: Italian Wikipedia gives 1893, English gives 1894 and names the Sorbonne; month unknown
stops.campa: Sent north out of Alexandria, he takes his baccalaureate in Paris, in the quarter of the Sorbonne. The city receives him as a colonial cousin with money, French without an accent, and an appetite for the little reviews. He reads the Symbolists and begins writing in their idiom, for their audience. Paris will keep calling him back for thirty years: he publishes here, duels here, and in 1909 buys the front page of its most respectable newspaper. The year of the diploma is contested. Italian sources give 1893, English ones 1894, and nothing consulted settles it.
suggested_refs: The Left Bank Symbolist reviews of the 1890s, first literary milieu of the young Marinetti

stops.name: Genoa, the law degree
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the city is contested, Italian Wikipedia gives Genoa and English gives Pavia, and no source consulted resolves it; month unknown
stops.campa: He takes his law degree in 1899, in the university quarter above the port, and never argues a case. His father wanted the credential; the son wanted Paris, verse, and a review of his own. He finishes the one thing his family can point to and then spends fifty years finishing manifestos instead. The law leaves him one habit: a taste for the drafted document that declares a state of affairs into being because it has been signed, dated and published. Italian sources put the degree at Genoa and English ones at Pavia.
suggested_refs: The law faculty in via Balbi, Genoa; and the rival Pavia attribution of the same 1899 laurea

stops.name: Paris, La Conquete des Etoiles
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month of publication and of his mother's death not established
stops.campa: His mother dies, and in the same year he publishes La Conquete des Etoiles in Paris, in French, a first book of verse under a Symbolism he has not yet decided to hate. The lines are cosmic and ornate, seas making war on stars, everything owed to the generation of Mallarme. Within seven years he will denounce this exact music in print, name moonlight as the enemy and call for its murder. Grief and publication arrive in the same twelve months. He writes nothing about the first.
suggested_refs: La Conquete des Etoiles (Paris, 1902), the Symbolist first book he later repudiated

stops.name: Creteil, the abbey of the communal poets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: sources record Marinetti only as an undated visitor, and the community ran from October 1906 to 28 January 1908
stops.campa: In a disused abbey at Creteil on the edge of Paris, a group of poets and printers keeps a press and a common table: art made outside the salons and outside the dealers. Albert Gleizes, Rene Arcos, Henri-Martin Barzun, Alexandre Mercereau and Charles Vildrac found it in October 1906 and it closes on the twenty-eighth of January 1908. Marinetti is recorded among its visitors, along with Brancusi. What he took from the place, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Abbaye de Creteil press, October 1906 to January 1908

segments.name: Milan, the Ditch, and the Front Page

stops.name: Corso Venezia, the offices of Poesia
stops.date_confidence: the review runs from 1905; the exact street number on Corso Venezia is not verified in sources consulted
stops.campa: From an apartment on Corso Venezia he founds and directs Poesia, an eclectic review that prints free verse out of half of Europe and pays for it from his father's estate. Editorial cards, an address list, a household run like a newsroom. After 1909 the same rooms serve as operational headquarters of a movement: letterhead, meetings, manifestos going out by post to any newspaper that will open the envelope. The founding manifesto opens with a night in these rooms, mosque lamps and men who have not slept.
stops.quote: We had stayed up all night, my friends and I, under hanging mosque lamps with domes of filigreed brass, domes starred like our spirits, shining like them with the prisoned radiance of electric hearts.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: Poesia (Milan, 1905-1909), later the house organ of Futurism

stops.name: The Monza road, the ditch
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the crash site was never precisely documented, secondary accounts also give October 1908, and the ditch imagery survives only in Marinetti's own telling
stops.campa: On a night in December he drives fast out of Milan, swerves to miss two cyclists, and puts the Isotta Fraschini into a drainage ditch full of factory water. He climbs out filthy and unhurt, and mechanics winch the car up by the wheels. Two months later the accident reappears as scripture at the head of the manifesto: the ditch as a mother, the factory sludge as milk, the driver hauled out of the mud and reborn with his heart on fire. Nobody else who was on that road has left an account of the night. He is thirty-two years old.
stops.quote: O maternal ditch, almost full of muddy water! Fair factory drain! I gulped down your nourishing sludge; and I remembered the blessed black breast of my Sudanese nurse…
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: The Isotta Fraschini of 1908, and the drainage ditches of Milan's northern industrial belt

stops.name: Bologna, the first newspaper printing
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Gazzetta dell'Emilia printing is the first in a newspaper, preceded in January 1909 by an appearance as preface to a volume of his poems in Milan; office address not verified, city-centre coordinates used
stops.campa: The manifesto's first newspaper printing happens here, on the front page of the Gazzetta dell'Emilia, on the fifth of February. It has already appeared in January as a preface to a volume of his own poems in Milan, read by almost nobody. Bologna prints it and Bologna forgets it: no riot follows, no telegram from abroad, no imitators by the weekend. He is testing the language on a provincial readership. The premiere he has arranged is two weeks away and six hundred kilometres north, and that is the version the century will keep.
suggested_refs: Gazzetta dell'Emilia, 5 February 1909, front page

stops.name: Rue Drouot, the front page of Le Figaro
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twentieth of February Le Figaro carries the Manifesto of Futurism on its front page, a placement he has arranged himself. Eleven numbered points renounce the museums, the libraries, the academies, moonlight and the adjective, and exalt speed, danger, the machine and war. He has chosen Paris because Paris turns a piece of writing into an international event overnight. Within weeks the word futurismo is being translated, mocked and copied on three continents. Most of the people using it have read the eleven points and nothing else.
stops.quote: We intend to sing the love of danger, the habit of energy and fearlessness.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism,' Le Figaro, 20 February 1909, trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: Le Figaro, 20 February 1909, front page, 'Le Futurisme'

stops.name: Paris, the premiere of Le Roi Bombance
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day not established; the Paris pin is the city's canonical point, the theatre is not named in sources consulted
stops.campa: His satirical drama Le Roi Bombance opens in Paris in April and the audience whistles it down from the first act. He answers one hostile critic in the only currency he considers adequate and fights him with a sword. The play is a five-act allegory of a revolution that eats itself, written years before the manifesto, and it is received as an impertinence by a public that has just read the eleven points and knows exactly who is demanding its attention. He counts the whistling as data.
suggested_refs: Le Roi Bombance (Paris, 1909) and the duel that followed its premiere

stops.name: Milan, the trial of Mafarka
stops.date_confidence: acquittal at first instance October 1910 attested; the acquittal was overturned on appeal and the conviction upheld by the Court of Cassation, dates of the later stages not established
stops.campa: His novel Mafarka il futurista, an African fable of a king who fathers a winged son without a woman, is prosecuted for obscenity. A court acquits him in October. The acquittal is overturned on appeal, and the conviction is then upheld by the Court of Cassation: three instances of Italian justice over one novel, begun the year he turns thirty-four. In the same year the painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carra and Luigi Russolo attach themselves to the movement.
suggested_refs: Mafarka il futurista (1910) and its obscenity prosecution through three instances

stops.name: Politeama Rossetti, Trieste
stops.date_confidence: the January 1910 date rests on Berghaus alone and is not corroborated by the theatre's own record; day unknown
stops.campa: The first great Futurist evening is staged at the Politeama Rossetti in Trieste, an Italian-speaking city under Habsburg administration. He reads manifestos to an audience assembled to jeer, and the jeering is the performance. The irredentist charge in the room costs him nothing to arrange, since it is already there, in the police at the back and in what half the hall wants Italy to do about this port. The evening ends in noise and he books the next one.
stops.quote: Art, in fact, can be nothing but violence, cruelty, and injustice.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: Politeama Rossetti, Viale XX Settembre 45, Trieste

stops.name: Teatro Lirico, Milan
stops.date_confidence: February 1910 is uncorroborated by the theatre's own record; day unknown
stops.campa: At the Teatro Lirico in via Larga the evening becomes a small riot: vegetables come over the footlights, fists are thrown in the aisles, the police are called. Marinetti, Boccioni, Carra and Russolo stand on the stage and insult the crowd back. The formula is now fixed and it will tour for a decade. Declaim, provoke, absorb the fruit, be arrested if the evening allows it, then read the outraged reviews aloud in the morning. What the audience does is the second half of the work.
suggested_refs: Teatro Lirico (now Teatro Lirico Giorgio Gaber), Via Larga 14, Milan

stops.name: Torre dell'Orologio, the leaflets over Venice
stops.date_confidence: the text Contro Venezia passatista is dated 27 April 1910; the leaflet action over Piazza San Marco is conventionally placed in July, day not established
stops.campa: From the Torre dell'Orologio above Piazza San Marco, thousands of leaflets go down onto the tourists and the gondoliers. The text is Contro Venezia passatista, written on the twenty-seventh of April by Marinetti with Boccioni, Carra and Russolo: fill in the canals, pull down the palaces, put a military port and a rail yard where the museum city stands. Venice, sold to the world as a corpse preserved in water, is the target he wants most, and he hits it from its own clock tower.
stops.quote: Museums: cemeteries!… Identical, surely, in the sinister promiscuity of so many bodies unknown to one another.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: Contro Venezia passatista (27 April 1910), signed by Marinetti, Boccioni, Carra and Russolo

stops.name: Tripoli, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He lands at Tripoli on the twelfth of October, days after the Italian fleet takes the port, as war correspondent for the Paris paper L'Intransigeant. For three years he has been writing that war is the world's only hygiene. Now he is standing in one, close enough to smell it, and filing to a readership that pays for the smell. The book he makes out of the dispatches, La battaglia di Tripoli, runs to thirty-eight thousand copies, more than anything Poesia ever printed.
stops.quote: We will glorify war—the world's only hygiene—militarism, patriotism, the destructive gesture of freedom-bringers, beautiful ideas worth dying for, and scorn for woman.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), point 9, trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: La battaglia di Tripoli (1912), collected from his L'Intransigeant dispatches

stops.name: Sciara Sciat, the oasis
stops.date_confidence: the battle of 23 October and the counterattack of 26 October are attested; the extent of Marinetti's own participation is disputed by biographers, and the coordinates are approximate
stops.campa: At the oasis of Sciara Sciat outside Tripoli, Ottoman regulars and Arab irregulars fall on the Italian line and cut down scores of soldiers. Marinetti says he took part in the counterattack of the twenty-sixth; biographers dispute how much of the fighting he saw. He turns the days into free-word prose: machine guns set as typography, shellfire as onomatopoeia, the dispatch and the poem coming out of the same notebook in the same hand. Italian reprisals follow across the oasis villages and kill Libyans in numbers nobody counted.
suggested_refs: The Sciara Sciat engagement of 23 October 1911 and the Italian reprisals that followed

stops.name: Milan, the words in freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Technical Manifesto of Futurist Literature goes out from Milan on the eleventh of May. Destroy syntax. Abolish the adjective and the adverb. Put every verb in the infinitive. Do away with punctuation and set the words loose. Parole in liberta: the page is to be a diagram of sensation rather than a sentence, typeface used as noise, the poet working like a telegraph operator under fire. He has been demanding the union of the man and the motor for a year already.
stops.quote: It is therefore necessary to prepare the imminent and inevitable identification of man with the motor, facilitating and perfecting an incessant exchange of intuition, rhythm, instinct and metallic discipline.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'Multiplied Man and the Reign of the Machine' (1911), quoted in Berghaus, International Futurism in Arts and Literature (2000), p. 318; located via Wikiquote, not verified against the printed page
suggested_refs: Manifesto tecnico della letteratura futurista, 11 May 1912

stops.name: Edirne, the siege lines
stops.date_confidence: his reporting visit falls in autumn 1912 and lasted weeks; the siege itself ran 3 November 1912 to 26 March 1913, and the two are often conflated
stops.campa: He goes out to the Bulgarian lines investing the Ottoman garrison at Adrianople, reporting the First Balkan War for the French press. The Bulgarians are shelling a city the Ottomans have held for five centuries. His own visit lasts weeks in the autumn of 1912; the siege itself will grind on until the following March. Out of the weeks within earshot of the guns comes Zang Tumb Tumb: shells set in type, telegraph static as verse, syntax abandoned on the grounds that the artillery abandoned it first. It is printed at Milan in 1914.
suggested_refs: Zang Tumb Tumb (Milan, 1914), the parole in liberta account of the Adrianople siege

stops.name: Biblioteca Universitaria di Pavia, the forty-two manifestos
stops.date_confidence: the donation was made between 1913 and 1916; exact dates of the individual deposits not established
stops.campa: Between 1913 and 1916, at the height of the movement, he gives the university library at Pavia forty-two Futurist manifestos, seven first editions of his own books, and works by Folgore, Buzzi, Papini, Palazzeschi and Govoni. The man who has demanded that libraries be burned deposits his own archive inside one: catalogued, shelved, temperature-controlled, and kept for exactly the scholars he has instructed to die. The Fondo Marinetti is still there.
suggested_refs: Fondo Marinetti, Biblioteca universitaria di Pavia, Strada Nuova 65

stops.name: Moscow, the Russian Futurists
stops.date_confidence: the 1914 Russian tour is attested; the month of the Moscow lectures is not established in sources consulted
stops.campa: He arrives in Moscow as the movement's ambassador and finds the Russian Futurists already in possession of their own manifestos, their own scandals and no intention of being anybody's province. Several of them hold that their futurism came first and owes him nothing, and the argument is conducted partly in print and partly across the lectern. He lectures. He is heckled in a language he does not speak. From Moscow he travels on to Petersburg, where the reception is cooler still.
suggested_refs: The 1914 Russian lecture tour and the Moscow Cubo-Futurists' response to it

segments.name: The Great War and the Fasci

stops.name: Piazza del Duomo, the Austrian flags
stops.date_confidence: the arrest is attested without a month; conventionally dated to mid-September 1914, and the frequent claim that it followed Sarajevo by weeks is wrong
stops.campa: In Piazza del Duomo he burns Austrian flags in front of a crowd and is arrested for it. Italy is neutral, and the interventionist campaign in the streets of Milan is being run by poets, syndicalists and a socialist editor named Mussolini who has just lost his party over the same question. Futurism has spent five years calling war the world's hygiene. Now its founder is in the square demanding one, and he will be in uniform within a year of getting it.
suggested_refs: The Milanese interventionist demonstrations of September 1914

stops.name: Riva del Garda, the volunteer cyclists
stops.date_confidence: service with the Lombard Volunteer Cyclist Battalion in 1915 is attested; the month and the sector along the Garda front are approximate
stops.campa: He enlists in the Lombard Volunteer Cyclist Battalion and serves on the Trentino front above Lake Garda, thirty-eight years old and refusing a desk. Bicycles in mountain country turn out to be exactly what they look like, and the volunteer cyclist units are broken up within months. He stays in uniform and transfers toward the artillery, which is at least a machine. The war he asked for in print arrives as mud and a bicycle pushed uphill. The month of his enlistment and the sector he held are not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Battaglione Volontari Ciclisti Lombardo on the Trentino front, 1915

stops.name: The Isonzo, Monte Kuk
stops.date_confidence: the bronze Medal of Military Valour for Monte Kuk, 12-14 May 1917, is attested; the exact place and date of his wounding on the Isonzo are not specified in sources consulted
stops.campa: On the Isonzo in May, serving with an artillery unit, he fights at Monte Kuk on the twelfth to the fourteenth and is given the bronze Medal of Military Valour. In the same season he is seriously wounded. The sources consulted do not say where he was hit, or on what day. He recovers and goes back to the guns, and for the rest of his life the wound is the answer he gives to men who theorized this war from a cafe. He is forty years old, and this is the second of the four wars he volunteers for.
suggested_refs: The Monte Kuk citation of May 1917 in Marinetti's list of decorations

stops.name: Vittorio Veneto, the armoured car
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the final Italian offensive he goes forward at Vittorio Veneto driving a Lancia 1Z armoured car, a poet at the wheel of the exact object his manifesto had ranked above Greek sculpture. The Austro-Hungarian army breaks, and the armistice on the Italian front is signed within a fortnight. He is forty-one years old and at the wheel himself. Within a year nationalist mouths have renamed the victory: la vittoria mutilata, a win stolen back at the conference table. The men organizing in Milan will find the grievance worth more than the triumph was.
stops.quote: A racing car whose hood is adorned with great pipes, like serpents of explosive breath, a roaring car that seems to ride on grapeshot is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), point 4, trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: The Lancia 1Z armoured car of the 1918 offensive

stops.name: Piazza San Sepolcro, the founding of the Fasci
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a hall off Piazza San Sepolcro, on the twenty-third of March, about a hundred men found the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento: syndicalists, arditi, veterans with nowhere to put the war. Marinetti is among them and co-writes the founding programme with the syndicalist Alceste De Ambris. It is a republican document: no crown, no Vatican privilege, the eight-hour day, a levy on war profits. The Futurist Political Party he founded the year before folds into the new movement. Mussolini chairs the meeting.
suggested_refs: The San Sepolcro programme of 23 March 1919, drafted with Alceste De Ambris

stops.name: Milan, the sacking of Avanti!
stops.date_confidence: attested; the 1919 address of the Avanti! offices is not verified in sources consulted and the coordinates approximate central Milan
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of April he leads arditi and Futurists against a socialist and anarchist march near the Duomo. Three young workers are killed. The same day the offices of Avanti!, the socialist daily Mussolini edited until the war split him from it, are stormed and burned. Later Fascist history will keep the afternoon as a founding legend and print the date in its calendars. In Marinetti's account it is Futurist theatre that has escalated into history. The presses are wrecked and the type is scattered across the street.
suggested_refs: The assault on the Avanti! offices, Milan, 15 April 1919

stops.name: Fiume, the poet's city
stops.date_confidence: his presence during D'Annunzio's occupation is attested; the exact dates of his stay, which lasted days, are not established
stops.campa: He goes to Fiume while Gabriele D'Annunzio holds it, drawn by the one place in Europe where a poet commands troops and writes a constitution for heroes. Legionaries, arditi, deserters, futurists and dreamers: the city is running as his manifestos described, without a state to answer to. D'Annunzio, who has never enjoyed sharing a balcony, asks him to leave within days. The two have circled one another since Paris, where Marinetti published a pamphlet called The Gods Depart, D'Annunzio Remains and meant it as a complaint.
suggested_refs: The Italian Regency of Carnaro at Fiume, September 1919 to December 1920

stops.name: Milan, the second congress and the walkout
stops.date_confidence: May 1920 attested for the break; the congress city is contested, Italian sources place the second congress of the Fasci at Milan and other accounts at Florence, and the day is not established
stops.campa: At the second congress of the Fasci he demands the movement keep its own word: no monarchy, no Church inside the state, svaticanare l'Italia. Mussolini is already trading those clauses for landowners, monarchists and priests, and the room votes accordingly. Marinetti walks out and stays out of organized politics for three years. He does not renounce Fascism; he renounces the meetings. The distinction will let him swallow a great deal later without ever admitting he changed his mind.
suggested_refs: The second congress of the Fasci di Combattimento, May 1920, and Marinetti's resignation

stops.name: Paris, the tactile tables
stops.date_confidence: the manifesto Il Tattilismo dates to 1921 and was first presented in Paris that January; the frequent 1923 date is contaminated from the year of his marriage
stops.campa: He presents Tattilismo in Paris in January: tables of sandpaper, silk, sponge, wire and velvet, built to be read by the hands with the eyes shut. The argument is that touch has been left illiterate for centuries while the eye was educated. Paris, which has had Dada in the meantime and is harder to startle than it was in 1909, receives the tactile tables coolly, and several of his own Futurists think the whole line a distraction from painting. He goes on making them anyway.
suggested_refs: Il Tattilismo. Manifesto futurista (1921), first presented in Paris

stops.name: Rome, the marriage to Benedetta Cappa
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the date and place of the ceremony are not specified in sources consulted, and Rome is given as the couple's settled residence
stops.campa: He marries Benedetta Cappa, painter, novelist and pupil of Giacomo Balla, whom he met in 1918. He marries her, by his own account, mainly to simplify a lecture tour to Brazil; the early manifestos had listed marriage alongside the museums among things due for abolition. Benedetta becomes his most serious collaborator and a leading exponent of the aeropainting still to come, and the household that grows around them is the ordinary thing his manifestos had no clause for. They settle in Rome and have three daughters: Vittoria, Ala and Luce.
suggested_refs: Benedetta Cappa Marinetti, painter and novelist, 1897-1977

stops.name: Bologna, the Congress of Fascist Culture
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At the Congress of Fascist Culture in Bologna, Giovanni Gentile names Marinetti's artistic and creative ideas among the springs of the movement, and Marinetti presses hard for the identification of Futurism with the regime's official style. The regime's own cultural apparatus prefers columns, eagles and imperial Rome, and says so out loud. The allegiance is not returned in the coin he is asking for. He signs the Manifesto of Fascist Intellectuals the same year.
suggested_refs: The Bologna Congress of Fascist Culture, 29-30 March 1925, and the Manifesto of Fascist Intellectuals

stops.name: Buenos Aires, futurism arrives in person
stops.date_confidence: the 1926 South American lecture tour is attested; the months and the individual venues in Buenos Aires are not established in sources consulted
stops.campa: Futurism reaches Argentina in the body of its founder. He lectures across Buenos Aires, in a city whose modernists have been arguing about him in print for years without ever having to look at him. The Florida writers and the crowd around Amigos del Arte turn out for a man whose ism they have already translated, localized and quarrelled over. The manifesto has been arriving in this city by post since 1909; this time it comes by steamer, with its author aboard. He speaks; they measure the man against the paper version.
suggested_refs: Marinetti's 1926 South American lecture tour and the Buenos Aires avant-garde reception

stops.name: Rome, the Accademia d'Italia
stops.date_confidence: the Academy was created by decree 7 January 1926, its first thirty members including Marinetti approved 13 March 1929, and it was inaugurated 28 October 1929; the coordinates approximate its Palazzo Corsini seat
stops.campa: Mussolini names him to the Royal Academy of Italy, created by decree three years earlier, its first thirty members approved in March and installed in October. He is issued the plumed hat, the ceremonial sword and the title of academician, with a stipend. Twenty years before he had put the academies on a list with the museums and the libraries, to be destroyed. The Futurists who stayed poor call it capitulation. He calls it a beachhead, and wears the sword.
stops.quote: We will destroy the museums, libraries, academies of every kind, will fight moralism, feminism, every opportunistic or utilitarian cowardice.
stops.quote_source: F.T. Marinetti, 'The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism' (1909), point 10, trans. R.W. Flint
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy of Italy at Palazzo Corsini alla Lungara, and its academician's uniform

stops.name: The Gulf of La Spezia, aeropittura
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month of the flight and of the manifesto's drafting is not established
stops.campa: Flying over the Gulf of La Spezia he drafts the manifesto of aeropittura. The aeroplane has abolished the horizon, the fixed viewpoint and the upright human body, and painting is instructed to be redone from the cockpit: spirals, dives, the coastline seen as a diagram. Half a century of Italian landscape painting is ordered into the air. Benedetta Cappa becomes one of the style's leading practitioners, and painters half his age take up a movement twenty years old.
suggested_refs: Manifesto dell'aeropittura futurista (1929)

stops.name: Turin, the manifesto against pasta
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Gazzetta del Popolo of Turin prints the Manifesto of Futurist Cooking on the twenty-eighth of December. Pasta is denounced as a cause of lassitude, pessimism and lack of virility; rice is proposed in its place. Meals are to be eaten while the free hand strokes sandpaper or velvet, perfume sprayed at the diner between courses, food eventually replaced by pills and plastic complexes. A handful of restaurants play along for the publicity. The pasta manufacturers write to the papers.
suggested_refs: Manifesto della cucina futurista, Gazzetta del Popolo, 28 December 1930

segments.name: The Last Wars and the Lake

stops.name: Passo Uarieu, the Ethiopian campaign
stops.date_confidence: the citations place him at Passo Uarieu on 21 January 1936 and at Uork Amba and Debek Amba on 27-28 February 1936, implying departure in 1935; coordinates approximate the northern front in Tigray
stops.campa: At fifty-nine he volunteers for the invasion of Ethiopia and goes out with the Second Blackshirt Division 28 Ottobre, ranked seniore. He is cited for the fighting at Passo Uarieu on the twenty-first of January and again at Uork Amba and Debek Amba at the end of February, and decorated for both. Three wars in, the doctrine still demands a body in the field, and he keeps supplying his own. Out of the campaign comes Il poema africano della Divisione 28 ottobre.
suggested_refs: Il poema africano della Divisione 28 ottobre; his Ethiopian decoration citations

stops.name: Rome, the last issue of Artecrazia
stops.date_confidence: the Artecrazia article is dated 11 January 1939; the degenerate-art intervention and the Racial Laws both fall in 1938
stops.campa: In 1938 he persuades Mussolini to keep the German exhibition of degenerate art out of Italy, the same year Italy passes its own Racial Laws in November. On the eleventh of January 1939 his journal Artecrazia defends Futurism against the regime's cultural hard line by insisting that the movement is Italian and nationalist, not foreign, and that there are no Jews in Futurism. The defence concedes the premise it is defending itself against. The regime closes the journal down anyway.
suggested_refs: Artecrazia, issue of 11 January 1939, and its suppression

stops.name: The middle Don, the ARMIR expedition
stops.date_confidence: his service in 1942 running into 1943 is attested; his unit's exact movements are not documented in sources consulted, and the coordinates stand for the Italian Eighth Army's Don sector rather than a place he is known to have stood
stops.campa: At sixty-five he volunteers for the Eastern Front and goes to Russia with the Italian expeditionary army holding the middle Don. He is decades older than any other volunteer in the sector, and he is there on doctrine: speed, war and machinery renew a man rather than use him up. The Soviet winter offensive destroys the Italian Eighth Army on that river. He was not at Stalingrad, whatever the later accounts say, and he comes home in 1943 ill and used up, dictating rather than writing from then on.
suggested_refs: The ARMIR on the middle Don, 1942-1943

stops.name: Bellagio, the Hotel Excelsior Splendide
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies of cardiac arrest at the Hotel Excelsior Splendide in Bellagio on the second of December, sixty-seven years old, in a lake town full of the functionaries of a republic with weeks left to run. He has just finished Quarto d'ora di poesia della X Mas, fifteen minutes of verse in praise of the naval commandos still fighting for Mussolini's Salo. He dies working, on the losing side of the fourth war he volunteered for. The sculptor Spartaco Di Ciolo takes a cast of his face. Where the mask went afterwards, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: Quarto d'ora di poesia della X Mas, his last completed work; the Di Ciolo death mask

stops.name: Bellagio, the service at San Giacomo
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinates of the basilica are approximate
stops.campa: The funeral is held the next day at the Basilica di San Giacomo in Bellagio, the Romanesque church on the hill above the water, before the body is taken south to Milan. This is the small service, the local one, for a man about to be given a state occasion by a state that barely exists any more. The mourners are hotel staff, local officials of the Republic, a widow and three daughters. It is December on Lake Como. The front line is two hundred kilometres off and will reach this shore inside five months.
suggested_refs: Basilica di San Giacomo, Bellagio, 3 December 1944

stops.name: Milan, the state funeral at San Sepolcro
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Italian Social Republic gives him a state funeral on the fifth of December at the church of San Sepolcro in Milan, in the same small square where the Fasci di Combattimento were founded twenty-five years earlier. Crowds come, in a city under Allied bombing and German garrison. The regime doing the burying has weeks of existence left, and the men in the honour guard know it as well as anyone in the pews. From the hall of the founding meeting to the door of the funeral church is about forty metres of Milanese pavement.
suggested_refs: Chiesa di San Sepolcro, Milan, state funeral of 5 December 1944

stops.name: Cimitero Monumentale, the grave
stops.date_confidence: burial at the Cimitero Monumentale attested; the exact date of interment and the tomb's design are not established in sources consulted
stops.campa: He is buried in the Cimitero Monumentale, among the industrialists, tenors and professors of the city whose past he had proposed to demolish. Benedetta Cappa, who dies at Venice in 1977, is laid beside him. No manifesto covered this part. The design of the tomb, and whether anything has happened to it since, the sources consulted do not establish. In 2014 the Guggenheim in New York mounts the first comprehensive American survey of Italian Futurism, 1909 to 1944.
suggested_refs: Cimitero Monumentale di Milano; 'Italian Futurism, 1909-1944: Reconstructing the Universe', Guggenheim, New York, 2014
